The current landscape of Artificial Intelligence is characterized by a complex interplay between technical development, economic investment, and operational stability. In terms of technical safety and alignment, the emergence of 'sycophancy' in Large Language Models (LLMs) has become a critical concern. Sycophancy is defined as the tendency for models to mirror a user's views regardless of the actual accuracy of the information provided. This phenomenon creates a significant challenge for alignment, which is the process of ensuring the model's outputs are aligned with human values and intentions. 

There is a persistent tension between 'capabilities'—defined as the model's power and utility—and 'safety'—the mitigation of risks associated with the model's output. Some safety interventions, while intended to prevent harm, can inadvertently degrade a model's performance or its core reasoning capabilities. To combat this, developers implement 'red teaming' and various guardrails to prevent the generation of harmful content. However, a known trade-off exists: over-tuning for safety can lead to 'refusal' behavior, where the model declines to answer even benign requests. 

Parallel to these technical hurdles, the economic landscape of AI in 2025 is marked by high concentration of capital. Global investment is led by the United States, which dominates in both the scale and volume of funding. In a comparison of private investment, the U.S. significantly exceeded the totals of other leading countries. This shift is evidenced by these increased funding for startups that integrate LLMs into specialized professional workflows. Despite the overall growth in funding, investors are becoming more discerning. block-L1-001.context:
The 2026 Artificial Intelligence Index Report, published in April 2026 by the AI Index Steering Committee of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) at Stanford University, is the ninth edition of the report. The AI Index is an independent initiative conceived within the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100).

### AI Capabilities and Performance

AI capability is accelerating and reaching a broader population. In 2025, industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models, and several of these models now meet or exceed human baselines on PhD-level science questions, multimodal reasoning, and competition mathematics. In a single year, performance on the SWE-bench Verified coding benchmark rose from 60% to nearly 100% of the human baseline. 

Researchers describe the current state of AI as a "jagged frontier," where models can achieve high-level specialized tasks but fail at simple ones. For example, Gemini Deep Think won a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO), yet the top AI model correctly reads analog clocks only 50.1% of the time. While AI agents improved their task success on OSWorld (which tests real computer tasks across operating systems) from 12% to approximately 66%, they still fail roughly one in three attempts on structured benchmarks. In robotics, a wide gap exists between controlled and unpredictable environments; robots succeed in only 12% of household tasks, whereas robotic manipulation in software-based simulations on RLBench has reached 89.4% success.

AI models for science are now capable of outperforming human scientists, though bigger models do not always perform better. Frontier models outperform human chemists on average on ChemBench, but these models score below 20% on replication in astrophysics and 33% on Earth observation questions. Specialized models have shown surprising efficiency: a 111-million-parameter protein language model, MSAPairformer, beat previous leading methods on ProteinGym, and a 200-million-parameter genomics model, GPN-Star, outperformed a model nearly 200 times larger. Most AI foundation models for science come from cross-sector collaborations, whereas general-purpose AI is dominated by industry.

### National Competition and Geopolitics

Regarding international competition, the performance gap between U.S. and Chinese AI models has effectively closed, with the two countries trading the lead multiple times since early 2025. In February 2025, DeepSeek-R1 briefly matched the top U.S. model, and as of March 2026, Anthropic’s top model leads by only 2.7%.

In terms of model production, the United States led in 2025 with 59 notable AI models, followed by China with 35 and South Korea with 8. Historically, from 2003–2025, the U.S. has produced the most notable models, with China producing 35 and Europe producing 2. Other countries producing one notable model in 2025 included Canada, France, Hong Kong, Singapore, and the United Kingdom.

While the U.S. leads in producing top-tier AI models and higher-impact patents, China leads in publication volume, citation share, and patent grants. South Korea leads the world in AI patents per capita (14.31 per 100,000 inhabitants), followed by Luxembourg (12.25) and China (6.95).

Switzerland and Singapore lead the world in AI researchers per capita.

### Investment, Talent, and Economic Impact

U.S. private AI investment reached $285.9 billion in 2025, which is more than 23 times the $12.4 billion invested in China—though the report notes that private investment figures likely understate China’s total AI spending due to government guidance funds. The U.S. also led in entrepreneurial activity in 2025 with 1,953 newly funded AI companies, which is more than 10 times the number of companies in the next closest country.

However, the U.S. is seeing a decline in its ability to attract global talent. The number of AI researchers and developers moving to the U.S. has dropped 89% since 2017, with an 80% decline in the last year alone. While the number of new AI PhDs in the U.S. and Canada increased 22% from 2022 to 2024, the PhDs contributing to that increase took jobs in academia rather than in industry.

Gender gaps in AI talent remain deeply entrenched with no meaningful progress since 2010; however, some countries show relatively higher female representation, such as Saudi Arabia (32.3%), Canada (29.6%), and Australia (30.1%).

### Adoption, Productivity, and Education

Organizational adoption of AI reached 88%, and 80% (4 in 5) of university students now use generative AI. Generative AI reached 53% population adoption within three years, a pace faster than the PC or the internet. Adoption correlates strongly with GDP per capita, though some countries show higher-than-expected adoption: Singapore (61%) and the United Arab Emirates (54%), while the U.S. ranks 24th at 28.3%.

The estimated annual value of generative AI tools to U.S. consumers reached $172 billion by early 2026, with the median value per user tripling between 2025 and 2026.

Productivity gains are appearing in customer support and software development (14% to 26%), but effects are weaker or negative in tasks requiring more judgment. AI agent deployment remains in single digits across nearly all business functions. In software development, U.S. developers aged 22 to 25 saw employment fall nearly 20% from 2024, while headcount for older developers continues to grow.

In education, over 80% of U.S. high school and college students use AI for school-related tasks, but only half of middle and high schools have AI policies in place, and just 6% of teachers say those policies are clear. Conversely, AI engineering skills are accelerating fastest in the United Arab Emirates, Chile, and South Africa.

### Technical Infrastructure and Hardware

Infrastructure and hardware supply chains remain highly centralized. The United States hosts 5,427 AI data centers—more than 10 times the amount hosted by any other country—and consumes the most energy for AI. Global AI compute capacity has grown roughly 3.3 times per year since 2022, reaching 17.1 million H100-equivalents. Nvidia accounts for over 60% of total compute (17.07M H100e), with Google, Amazon, AMD, and Huawei each contributing approximately 1.88M H100e.

Hardware adoption for notable models is centered on specific accelerators. By 2025, 84 notable models were trained on A100-class hardware, 69 on V100, 44 on TPU v3, 28 on TPU v4, 28 on H100, 4 on H800, and 6 on P100, with another 54 models using other accelerators.

Global hardware supply chain depends heavily on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) from SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron, and fiber-optic connectivity via InfiniBand. Fabrication is almost entirely dependent on the Taiwanese company TSMC, which produces virtually every leading chip, including Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs and AMD's MI300X. While a TSMC-U.S. expansion began operations in 2025, the dependency remains critical.

### Model Production, Transparency, and Open Source

In 2025, Epoch AI identified 102 notable AI models. Industry produced 91.18% of these (93 models), while academia produced only two. The top organizational contributors in 2025 were OpenAI (20), Google (14), Alibaba (11), Anthropic (7), DeepSeek (5), xAI (4), LG AI Research (4), and Meta (4). Historically, Google has produced the most notable models (193), followed by Meta (87), OpenAI (60), Nvidia (42), and Alibaba (30). In academia, Tsinghua University (26), Stanford University (26), and Carnegie Mellon University (25) have been the most prolific over the past decade.

Release patterns are shifting toward controlled access. In 2025, 47 of 102 models were released via API access (the most common type since 2020). Other release types include "open weights (noncommercial)" (19), "hosted access (no API)" (14), "open weights (unrestricted)" (13), "open weights (restricted use)" (13), 27 were unreleased, and 10 were unknown.

Transparency is declining. In 2025, 81 of 102 notable models were released without their corresponding training code, and only four models were released with "open source" training code. Training code, dataset sizes, parameter counts, and training duration are often withheld by organizations such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Historically, parameter counts grew exponentially from the early 2010s through 2022, but reported growth has flattened since 2022 because these organizations no longer publicly disclose these metrics.

Regarding open-source development, AI-related GitHub projects grew from 1,549 in 2011 to 5.58 million in 2025, with a 23.7% year-over-year growth from 2024. However, most are experimental; only 206,880 projects in 2025 had 10 or more stars. Among these significant projects, the U.S. share declined from nearly 80% in 2011 to 31.71% in 2025, while Europe (24.47%), the Rest of the World (27.63%), China (11.01%), and India (5.18%) have grown. Despite this, the U.S. remains the most engaged, with 30.02 million cumulative GitHub stars for AI projects crossing the 10-star threshold, followed by the Rest of the World (15.27 million), Europe (12.99 million), China (9.00 million), and India (2.50 million).

Complementing GitHub, Hugging Face uploads have tripled since 2023. Model uploads rose from 3,000 in 2022Q1 to 332,000 in 2025Q4, and dataset uploads rose from 3,000 to 153,000. In terms of download share for the top 200 most-downloaded models (representing 49.6% of normalized downloads), as of 2025Q3, the U.S. holds a 17% share, followed by unaffiliated users (14%), International/Online (12%), China (12%), and the UK (11%). Modality trends on Hugging Face have shifted: text embedders and classifiers (down from 57.46% in 2022 to 2.71% in 2025) and audio models (down from 10.82% in 2022 to 2.88% in 2025) have been replaced by text generation (42.46%), image generation (25.61%), and multimodal generation (13.30%).

### Training Compute, Data, and Scaling

Training compute requirements for notable models have risen by several orders of magnitude. Key models tracked in training compute (measured in petaFLOP) include GPT-3 175B (davinci), ERNIE 3.0 Titan, GPT-4 (Mar 2023), Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Grok-2, Grok 4, DeepSeek-V3, Doubao-pro, Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen3-Max, and GLM-4.6.

As the industry approaches "peak data"—the point where high-quality human text and web data is exhausted—Epoch AI projects the depletion date to fall between 2026 and 2032. To combat this, researchers are exploring synthetic data. While synthetic data can accelerate training by 5 to 10 times through hybrid approaches, there is no definitive evidence it can fully replace real-world data in pre-training for general-purpose models. The SYNTHLLM family of models, trained entirely on synthetic data, performs well but still lags behind leading models. Synthetic data remains highly effective for post-training (fine-tuning and reinforcement learning), particularly for reasoning and long-context capabilities.

However, the rise of AI-generated content is evident; by January 2025, 51.72% of newly published online content was AI-generated, while human-generated content fell to 48.28%.

Due to the limitations of synthetic data, frontier labs are pivoting toward proprietary data, as seen in the May 2025 licensing agreement between the New York Times and Amazon, and similar strategic pursuits by Meta and health/life sciences firms like Bristol Myers Squibb.

Data-centric methods focused on quality over quantity have shown significant gains. The Olmo 3.1 Think 32B model, with roughly 32 billion parameters (nearly 90 times fewer than Grok 4's 3 trillion parameters), achieved competitive results on the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) 2025. Performance on AIME 2025 was: GPT-5 (high) at 94.3%, Gemini 1.5 Pro at 95.7%, Grok-4 at 92.7%, Claude Opus 4.5 at 91.3%, and OLMo 3 at 78.1%.

### Environmental and Social Impact

AI's environmental footprint is expanding. In 2025, Grok 4's estimated training emissions reached 72,816 tons of CO2 equivalent, far exceeding the lifetime emissions of an average car (63 tons). Other training emissions include Llama 3.1 405B (8,930 tons), GPT-4 (5,184 tons), Megatron-Turing NLG (1,432 tons), and GPT-3 (588 tons). For comparison, training AlexNet in 2012 produced only 0.01 tons of CO2 equivalent.

Inference energy and carbon footprints are also significant. For medium-length prompts (1,000 input/output tokens), DeepSeek V3.2 Exp and V3.2 consumed the most energy (23.24 Wh and 23.13 Wh, respectively) and produced the highest carbon emissions (13.95 gCO2e and 13.88 gCO2e). In contrast, Claude 4 Opus consumed 5.32 Wh and produced 1.6 gCO2e, while Mistral Medium 3 produced the lowest emissions at 1.52 gCO2e. At a per-query level, a short GPT-4o query consumes 0.42 Wh, which is 40% more than a Google search (0.3 Wh). A daily session of eight medium-length queries costs 9.71 Wh, which is comparable to charging two smartphones (10 Wh).

Water consumption for GPT-4o inference is estimated between 1,334,991 and 1,579,680 kiloliters annually, exceeding the drinking water needs of 1.2 million people (1,314,000 kL).

AI data center power capacity rose to 29.56 GW, a level comparable to New York state at peak demand (approx. 31 GW), the Netherlands (approx. 20 GW), and New Zealand (approx. 7 GW). Of this total, 11.82 GW was attributed to AI chip power (TDP), while 17.74 GW was for supporting infrastructure (cooling, networking).

Cumulative power demand for AI accelerator modules through 2024 reached approximately 5,200 MW, with the total all-in AI system demand (including servers and cooling) reaching 9,400 MW. This is comparable to the national electricity consumption of Switzerland (15,000 MW) or Austria (15,000 MW), and roughly half that of Bitcoin mining (25,000 MW), while total global data center demand (excluding crypto) is estimated at 47,000 MW.

Regional electricity consumption for data centers has increased across all major regions, with the United States holding the largest share, followed by China, Europe, and the the rest of Asia.

Regarding societal perspectives, there is a 50-point gap between experts and the public on AI's future. While 73% of experts expect a positive impact on how people do their jobs, only 23% of the public does. Trust in governments to regulate AI varies; the United States reported the lowest level of trust in its own government to regulate AI at 31%, while the EU is trusted more than the U.S. or China to regulate AI effectively.

### Clinical Care and Responsible AI

AI is transforming clinical care, with tools that automatically generate clinical notes from patient visits seeing substantial adoption in 2025. Physicians reported up to 83% less time spent writing notes and reduction in burnout. However, the evidence base for clinical AI remains thin; a review of more than 500 clinical AI studies found that nearly half relied on exam-style questions rather than real patient data, and only 5% used real clinical data.

Responsible AI is not keeping pace with technical capabilities. While almost all frontier model developers report capability benchmarks, reporting on responsible AI benchmarks is inconsistent. Documented AI incidents increased to 362 in 2025, up from 233 in 2024. AI incidents are further complicated by the research indicating that improving one responsible AI dimension, such as safety, may degrade another, such as accuracy.

### Global AI Patent Trends

Granted AI patents grew exponentially from 3,866 in 2010 to 131,121 in 2024. China dominates this landscape, accounting for 74.24% of global patents (97.99 thousand), followed by the U.S. (12.06%, 15.92 thousand), and the Rest of the World (10.35%, 13.66 thousand). In 2024, South Korea had the highest per capita patent rate (14.31 per 100,000 inhabitants), followed by Luxembourg (12.25) and China (6.95).

Despite China's volume, the U.S. maintains high downstream influence, according to forward citations. The U.S. accounts for 51.91% of forward citations (compared to China's 29.81%), and only 19% of U.S. patents remain uncited after 10 years, compared to 44% for Chinese patents.

Technological proximity analysis shows most countries align with both the U.S. and China, though Denmark is an outlier with only 52% overlap with the U.S. and and 45% with China, due to its focus on energy and wind-related technology (codes Y02E, F03D, F05B).

Example patents include Chinese patent CN111431996A (resource configuration using ML), U.S. patent US11436777B1 (hazard visualization), and U.S. patent US202323945 la (VR/AR stereoscopic view synthesis).

### Academic Research and Publications

AI publications in computer science (CS) more than doubled between 2013 and 2024, from roughly 102,000 to 257.89 thousand, representing 40.9% of all CS publications in OpenAlex. In 2024, journals were the primary venue (47%), followed by conferences (23.5%). Total attendance at 16 major AI conferences in 2025 reached 101.12 thousand, with NeurIPS (26.38k), ICLR (11.04k), and CVPR (9.38k) being the largest.

Geographically, China produced 17.76% of AI publications in 2024, followed by the Rest of the World (17.10%), Europe (11.05%), India (7.55%), and the United States (7.29%), though 39.25% of publications had an unknown country affiliation. In terms of citations, China led with 20.6%, followed by Europe (19.5%) and the U.S. (12.6%).

Sectorally, academia produced 68.13% of 2024 publications, following by government (12.44%) and industry (11.47%). In the U.S., industry's share was higher (24.46%) than in China (17.96%), while China's government sector was more significant (25.10%). Europe had the highest academic share at 55.3%.

Research remains concentrated in machine learning (37%), computer vision (22.4%), pattern recognition (11.나), and natural language processing (10%).

The most-cited publications from 2021-2024 show a shift in influence. The U.S. share of the top 100 publications declined from 64 (2021) to 46 (2024), while China's rose from 33 (2021) to 41 (2024) and Australia's rose from 2 (2021) to 14 (2024).

In 2024, Google and Stanford University led with 7 top-cited publications each, followed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Microsoft (5 each)."},

Talent mobility in 2025 was characterized by net flows. The United States remained net positive, though its flow decreased from a 2022 peak of 324.6 to 26.0 in 2025. Other positive flow countries included the UK (5.17), Saudi Arabia (3.08), Spain (2.58), the UAE (2.58), and Denmark (2.08), with Switzerland at 0.25. Italy, Japan, and France (0.08) had near-zero flow. Negative flow countries included India (-16.92), Canada (-7.08), Brazil (-3.58), Singapore (-2.58), Israel (-1.92), Australia (-1.75), South Korea (-1.75), Finland (-1.08), Germany (-2.42), and Sweden (-0.58). Canada's inflow peaked around 2020 before declining to -7.08.

### Technical Performance of Frontier AI Models

#### Model Benchmarks and Human Baselines
By 2025, frontier systems reached or exceeded human levels (100% baseline) on ImageNet (image classification), SuperGLUE (English language understanding), MMLU (multitask language understanding), MMMU (multimodal reasoning), GPQA Diamond (PhD-level science), and AIME (mathematical reasoning). However, gaps persist in autonomous software engineering (SWE-bench Verified) and agent-based multimodal computer use (OSWorld). While these are below human baseline, improvement is accelerating; SWE-bench Verified performance rose from ~60% in 2024 to nearly 100% in 2025.

#### Capability Convergence and Competition
As of March 2026, leading models have converged in capability. The Arena Elo ratings show the top tier is dominated by six companies: Anthropic (1,503), xAI (1,495), Google (1,494), OpenAI (1,481), Alibaba (1,449), and DeepSeek (1,424). The top four are separated by fewer than 25 Elo points. Other notable scores include Mistral AI (1,416) and Meta (1,335), with Meta's performance flattening since early 2025. 

Competition has shifted from raw capability to cost, reliability, and real-world utility. The gap between closed-weight and open-weight models fluctuates. In May 2023, GPT-4-0314 (closed) led Vicuna-13B (open) by 174 points (15.2%). By August 2024, models like Llama-3.1-405B, Mixtral, and WizardLM narrowed this gap to 7 points (0.5%). As of March 2026, Claude Opus 4.6 (closed, 1,503) leads GLM-5 (open, 1,454) by 49 points (3.4%).

#### U.S. vs. China Technical Performance
The technical gap between the U.S. and China has effectively closed. In February 2025, DeepSeek-R1 (Chinese) briefly matched the top U.S. model. In March 2026, the top U.S. model (Claude Opus 4.6, 1,503) led the top Chinese model (Dola-Seed-2.0 Preview, 1,464) by 39 points (2.7%). Over the past year, this gap has fluctuated between near parity and low single digits.

#### Language Capabilities and MMLU-Pro
To prevent memorization and reduce prompt sensitivity, the MMLU-Pro benchmark (introduced 2024) uses 12,000 questions in a 10-option multiple-choice format. Accuracy on MMLU-Pro is generally 16%–33% lower than on the original MMLU. As of early 2026, the top 15 models are clustered above 87%, with only a 4 percentage point spread. Gemini-3.1-Pro leads with 91.16%, followed by Gemini-3-Pro (11/25) at 90.10% and GPT-o1 at 89.30%. 

Full MMLU-Pro rankings:
- Gemini-3.1-Pro: 91.16%
- Gemini-3-Pro (11/25): 90.10%
- GPT-o1: 89.30%
- Claude-4.6-Opus (Thinking): 89.10%
- Gemini-3-Flash (12/25): 88.60%
- Qwen3.5-397B-A17B: 87.80%
- Seed2.0-Lite: 87.70%
- Claude-4.5-Sonnet (Thinking): 87.40%
- GPT-5.2: 87.40%
- Claude-4-Opus (Thinking): 87.30%
- Claude-4.5-Opus (Thinking): 87. uma 87.30%
- Hunyuan-T1: 87.20%
- K2.5-1T-A32B: 87.10%
- GPT-5 (high): 87.10%
- Grok-4: 87.00%

In the Text Arena, Claude-Opus-4-6-Thinking leads with an Elo of approximately 1,510, followed by Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. Other top models include Claude-opus-4-5-20251101 (~1,460), Grok-4.1 (~1,458), Gemini-3-flash (thinking-minimal) (~1,455), Claude-sonnet-4-6 (~1,452), and GPT-5.1-high (~1,450).

#### Benchmarking Limitations and "Jagged Intelligence"
Benchmarking is hindered by benchmark saturation, opacity in reporting, and contamination. A notable example was the criticism of Meta's Llama 4 in 2025 for being optimized specifically for benchmarks. 

Technical audits revealed high error rates in invalid question detection (precision@50). For MMLU Math and OpenBookQA, the error rate is 2%; for MMLU Cli and MMLU Med, it is 6%; for AIR-Bench, it is 9%; for MedQA, it is 23%; for ThaiExam, it is 26%; and for GSM8K, it is 42%. 

To combat these, new frameworks have been proposed: a statistical analysis framework by Truong et al. (2025) with 84% precision in flagging problematic items, and a 'certificate-grade' community-governed framework by Cheng et al. (2025).

Models exhibit "jagged intelligence," where they excel at complex tasks but fail at simple ones. For example, Gemini Deep Think won a gold medal at the 2025 IMO (35 points), but on ClockBench, top AI models read analog clocks correctly only 50.6% of the time (humans are 90.1%).

#### Domain-Specific and Agent Performance
- **Coding**: Models struggle with multi-step reasoning and long-horizon tasks. The 'CodeContests' benchmark is used to evaluate efficiency and correctness against hidden test cases.
- **Mathematics**: A gap remains between simple arithmetic (System 1) and complex problem-solving (System 2). MATH and GSM8K are used for assessments.
- **Professional Domains**: Performance in corporate finance, mortgage processing, tax, and legal reasoning is between 60% and 90%, with top models separated by as little as 3 percentage points. 
- **AI Agents**: Accuracy on OSWorld rose from 12% to 66.3%, currently within 6 percentage points of human performance.
- **Robotics**: A massive 'sim-to-real' gap exists. RLBench shows high simulation success rates (89.4%), but real-world household task success is only 12%.
- **Autonomous Vehicles**: In 2025, Waymo conducted ~450,000 weekly trips, and China's Apollo Go completed 11 million fully driverless rides (a 175% YoY increase).

#### Timeline of Major Releases (2025-2026)
- **DeepSeek-R1 (Jan 20, 2025)**: Uses GRPO for reinforcement learning without labeled data. Its release triggered a trillion-dollar market value decline in U.S. tech stocks.
- **Gemini 2.5 Pro (Mar 25, 2025)**: Multimodal model with 1M tokens context, scored ~63.8% on SWE-Bench Verified.
- ** uma 2025 (Sep 29, 2025)**: Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved 61.4% on OSWorld and 77.2%+ on SWE-bench Verified.
- **GPT-5.1 (Nov 12, 2025)**: A faster multimodal model scoring ~76.3% on SWE-bench Verified (vs. ~72.8%).

#### Software Layer Failures
The report identifies software layer errors, such as the 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'model_dump' error, as indicators of code execution errors in the software layer interacting with the LLM.

### Summary of Evaluation Paradigms
To move beyond synthetic benchmarks, researchers are proposing 'Centaur evaluations' to measure human-AI collaboration and interpretability, and addressing the 'sim-to-real' gap in robotics via domain randomization and the scaling of training data.

block-L1-003.context:
The current state of Artificial Intelligence is defined by a complex interplay between technical development, economic investment, and operational stability. This landscape is characterized by a significant tension between 'capabilities'—the model's utility and power—and 'safety'—the mitigation of risks associated with the model's output. Some safety interventions, while intended to prevent harm, can inadvertently degrade a model's core reasoning capabilities or its overall performance. To mitigate these risks, developers implement 'red teaming' and various guardrails to prevent the generation of harmful content. However, a known trade-off exists where over-tuning for safety can lead to 'refusal' behavior, where the model declines to answer even benign requests.

Technical safety and alignment are further complicated by the emergence of 'sycophancy' in Large Language Models (LLMs), which is defined as the tendency for models to mirror a user's views regardless of the same same actual accuracy of the information. This creates a significant challenge for the process of alignment, which aims to ensure that model outputs are aligned with human values and intentions.

From an economic perspective, the AI landscape in 2025 is marked by a high concentration of capital. Global investment is led by the United States, which dominates in both the scale and volume of funding. In comparisons of private investment, the U.S. significantly exceeded the totals of other leading countries. This dominance is further evidenced by the number of AI 'unicorns'—startups valued over $1 billion—where the U.S. maintains a dominant lead, acting as a proxy for the intensity of private capital flow. Growth in the sector is driven primarily by a small number of high-valuation firms, with a notable shift in investment trends moving from general-purpose AI research toward 'applied AI' and 'vertical AI'. Vertical AI refers to solutions tailored for specific industries such as healthcare, law, and finance, evidenced by increased funding for startups that integrate LLMs into specialized professional workflows. Despite this overall growth, investors are now demanding clearer paths to profitability and revenue generation, rather than funding based on technical novelty alone.

In the realm of autonomous vehicles, the United States has experienced a mix of growth and challenges. While mileage for robotaxis has increased in cities like Phoenix and San Francisco, safety incidents have prompted some industry players to re-evaluate the timeline for 'driverless' or 'Level 4' autonomy. This reflects a broader tension between the rapid deployment of AI systems and the development of safety frameworks. There is a noted gap between deployment speed and the same-time development of corresponding safety benchmarks or oversight mechanisms, where many organizations are integrating AI but only a smaller fraction have established rigorous safety benchmarks.

Parallel to these operational challenges, AI governance is characterized by a global gap in enforcement. The integration of AI into scientific research in 2025 is characterized by a transition from AI as a simple data analysis tool to a collaborative partner in the hypothesis-generation process. This shift is formalised as the 'AI-for-Science' (AI4Science) paradigm, AI models are now trained specifically on scientific data rather than general text. In physics, AI is helping to analyze massive datasets from particle accelerators and telescopes that would be impossible for humans to process manually. In materials science, AI suggests thousands of candidate materials, which are then validated by human researchers in a lab.

Within the biological and health sciences, there is a significant focus on the intersection of AI and genomics. AI models are used to predict protein folding and genomic sequences, which directly accelerates drug discovery. This is achieved through the application of 'protein languages,' where LLMs treat amino acid sequences as tokens to predict functional sites and mutations. Furthermore, the application of geometric deep learning (GDL) has enabled more precise modeling of 3D molecular structures. This is critical for understanding how small molecules bind to proteins, which in turn improves the accuracy of virtual screening processes.

There is a notable trend toward the use of smaller, specialized models that can outperform larger, general-purpose models in molecular and biological discovery. To further enhance capabilities, there is a growing trend toward integrating multimodal data—combining text, image, and genomic data—to improve the ability to predict protein functions and drug-target interactions. In biological research, the 'Open-set' approach is specifically utilized to analyze cellular behavior.

In the medical sector, AI application is characterized by a tension between technological promise and real-world implementation. While AI is being applied to clinical tasks, such as clinical decision support and the automation of diagnostic tasks, there remains a significant gap in the actual deployment of these tools in real-world medical settings and healthcare workflows. Consequently, there is a a heavy emphasis on the necessity of evaluating these models for safety, reliability, and clinical efficacy before widespread adoption.

In the realm of earth sciences, AI is integrated into climate modeling to bridge the gap between coarse-grained global climate models and high-resolution local weather patterns. This is accomplished via machine learning 'emulators' which replace computationally expensive physics-based simulations, allowing for faster and more frequent climate projections. Additionally, AI is utilized in satellite imagery analysis to track deforestation and urban sprawl in real-time.

Crucially, the 'AI-for-Science' paradigm is being operationalized through the development of closed-loop systems. These systems integrate AI with robotics, such as lab-on-a-chip systems, creating a 'predict-synthesize-test-analyze' cycle. In this loop, the AI proposes a hypothesis, robots conduct the experiment, and the results are fed back into the AI to refine the model. This has led to the emergence of 'AI scientists'—agents capable of hypothesis generation and experimental design—which has significantly reduced the time required for lead optimization in drug discovery compared to traditional manual methods.

block-L0-013.context:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within the healthcare sector is characterized by a complex interplay between rapid technical deployment, regulatory frameworks, and the clinical utility of these tools. While AI integration is manifesting across both clinical and administrative domains, there exists a a persistent gap between regulatory approval and actual clinical utility; many AI tools have received official approval, but their tangible impact on patient outcomes remains a subject of ongoing study. 

In the clinical domain, AI is being deployed for diagnostic and patient management purposes to improve overall outcomes and efficiency. This is most evident in specialized medical imaging and pathology, where AI-driven tools have shown promise in reducing error rates and increasing the speed of diagnosis. Specifically, clinical applications have emerged in several key areas: 

1. Radiology: AI is utilized for the detection of nodules in lung CT scans and the identification of fractures in X-rays. The training of these models varies significantly in scale; for instance, some radiology AI models are trained on massive datasets containing up to 100,000 images, while other more specialized models rely on significantly smaller datasets. 

2. Pathology: AI is applied to the automated counting of cells and the grading of tumors, streamlining processes that were previously manual and time-consuming.

3. Cardiology: AI is employed for the analysis of ECGs to detect arrhythmias.

Beyond diagnostics, AI-driven predictive analytics are being employed to identify high-risk patients and facilitate proactive interventions, a strategy intended to reduce hospital readmission rates. In administrative domains, AI focus shifts toward the optimization of workflows and resource allocation to enhance operational efficiency.

To mitigate the risks associated with these autonomous analyses, the industry employs 'human-in-the-loop' systems. In these configurations, the AI provides a first-pass analysis that is subsequently verified by a clinician. This human oversight is essential to ensure safety and accuracy, specifically to reduce the frequency of false positives and false negatives.

From a regulatory perspective, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has experienced a surge in AI-enabled medical device submissions. A notable shift in regulatory strategy has emerged with the introduction of 'Predetermined Change Control Plans' (PCCPs). These plans allow manufacturers to specify in advance how an algorithm will be updated post-market, thereby eliminating the need for a new regulatory submission for every minor technical tweak or update to the algorithm.

Despite the technical potential, the widespread adoption of these tools is contingent upon solving several critical challenges. A primary concern is the necessity of 'algorithmic transparency' and 'explainability' (XAI). Clinicians are more likely to adopt and trust AI tools if the system can provide a a clear rationale for its output—for example, by highlighting the specific regions of a medical image or the specific data points that led to a particular diagnosis. Furthermore, the integration of AI into existing clinical workflows must be managed carefully to prevent increasing clinician burnout. Other systemic hurdles include the ongoing need to address data privacy concerns and the mitigation of algorithmic bias to ensure equitable patient care. This reflects a broader tension between the efficiency gains provided by AI and the necessity of rigorous human oversight to maintain patient safety.
block-L0-013.summary: AI in healthcare is being deployed in radiology (lung CT nodules/X-ray fractures), pathology (cell counting/tumor grading), and cardiology (ECG arrhythmia detection), with radiology models trained on up to 100,000 images. Regulatory trends shift toward FDA Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) for post-market updates and the use of 'human-in-the-loop' verification to reduce false positives/negatives.

This disconnect is mirrored in the same way in academic focus; while general computer science (CS) remains a staple of technical education, there is a growing emphasis on AI-specific literacy and specialized degrees. However, the integration of AI into K-12 and higher education curricula varies wildly by region. Some areas are aggressively integrating generative AI tools, while others lag behind.

In the United States, the healthcare and finance sectors are leading the adoption of AI-driven workflows, though regulatory hurdles remain. Simultaneously, the global workforce is experiencing a 'skills gap,' where the demand for AI-competent professionals far outstrips the supply of graduates from traditional computer science programs. To bridge this gap, there has been an increase in short-term certifications and 'bootcamp' style learning, which exist alongside traditional academic degrees such as Bachelor's, Master's, and professional certifications. These shorter, specialized certification programs are becoming a key method for rapid skill acquisition in a market where the demand for AI skills is growing rapidly.

Demographic disparities remain a central challenge in technical education. There is a significant disparity in gender representation across various technical fields and AI-related degrees. In the U.S. specifically, the state of K-12 computer science education shows mixed progress. While the percentage of schools offering computer science courses is growing, there is a notable disparity in the quality and availability of these courses across different demographics. Specifically, in the U20 population, there is a significant gap in computer science enrollment. In some regions or demographics, the enrollment rate is significantly lower than in others. While student interest in computer science remains high, the transition from introductory courses to advanced coursework is a critical bottleneck, often hindered by a lack of qualified teachers and systemic barriers.

At the higher education level, universities are adapting to the prevalence of generative AI. University policies are evolving from outright bans to guided integration, with an emphasis on the need for AI literacy among both students and faculty. This shift is focused on policy development, the shift toward AI-assisted learning, and the challenge of maintaining academic integrity.

From a global perspective, there is a trend of 'AI Sovereignty.' Nations such as France, the UAE, and China are investing billions of dollars into domestic compute clusters and foundational models to reduce dependency on US-based providers like OpenAI, Google, and Meta. This geopolitical shift is driving a diversification of the hardware supply chain, which currently remains heavily reliant on NVIDIA GPUs. 

Regarding the integration of AI into national curricula, some countries are more aggressive than the United States. For example, China and several European nations have introduced AI modules at the primary and secondary education levels. In contrast, the U.S. faces a significant gap in AI education; while the government has begun emphasizing AI literacy at the policy level, there is a lack of standardized AI curricula in schools, and implementation varies widely. 

Across all levels of education, a fundamental pedagogical challenge remains: while technical tools are available, the pedagogical framework for teaching AI—balancing theory, ethics, and practice—remains underdeveloped. Furthermore, industry-led initiatives often fill the gap where public education falls short, but this frequently leads to an uneven distribution of AI skills across different socioeconomic groups.

This indicates a technical failure in the backend processing of the response, which prevents the user from receiving the expected structured data in a valid JSON format matching a required schema. This failure is often a result of a previous interaction failing due to a Python-related crash in the last response generation process, likely during a model's internal data structure conversion to JSON.

Finally, the current state of AI governance is characterized by a global gap in enforcement. While several jurisdictions have begun introducing AI-specific legislation to mandate transparency and risk assessments, global governance approaches vary by jurisdiction. Some nations adopt a 'light-touch' approach to foster industry growth and innovation, while others move toward mandatory compliance and certification processes designed to ensure public safety and trust. This is most evident in the emergence of specific AI acts and guidelines, such as those in the European Union (EU), specifically the EU AI Act, which aims to categorize AI risks and mandate audits for high-risk systems.

block-L1-005.context:
The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in 2025 is characterized by a complex interplay between technical deployment, regulatory frameworks, and the socio-educational landscape. In the healthcare sector, AI's adoption is marked by a persistent gap between regulatory approval and actual clinical utility; while many tools have received official approval, their tangible impact on patient outcomes remains a subject of ongoing study. AI is being deployed across both clinical and administrative domains to improve overall outcomes and efficiency. In the clinical domain, AI-driven tools have shown promise in reducing error rates and increasing the speed of diagnosis, particularly in specialized medical imaging and pathology.

Specifically, clinical applications of AI in healthcare have emerged in several key areas: 

1. Radiology: AI is utilized for the detection of nodules in lung CT scans and AI-driven tools are used for the identification of fractures in X-rays. The scale of training data varies significantly; some radiology AI models are trained on massive datasets containing up to 100,000 images, while other more specialized models rely on significantly smaller datasets.

2. Pathology: AI is applied to the automated counting of cells and the grading of tumors, streamlining processes that were previously manual and time-consuming.

3. Cardiology: AI is employed for the analysis of ECGs to detect arrhythmias.

Beyond diagnostics, AI-driven predictive analytics are being used to AI-driven predictive analytics are being employed to identify high-risk patients and facilitate proactive interventions, with the specific goal of reducing hospital readmission rates. In administrative domains, the focus shifts toward the optimization of workflows and resource allocation to enhance operational efficiency. To mitigate the risks of autonomous analyses, the industry employs 'human-in-the-loop' systems, where AI provides a first-pass analysis that is subsequently verified by a clinician to reduce the frequency of false positives and false negatives.

From a regulatory perspective, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has seen a surge in AI-enabled medical device submissions. A notable shift in regulatory strategy has emerged with the introduction of 'Predetermined Change Control Plans' (PCCPs), which allow manufacturers to specify in advance how an algorithm will be updated post-market, eliminating the need for a new regulatory submission for every minor technical tweak or update.

Despite these advancements, widespread adoption is contingent upon solving critical challenges. A primary concern is the necessity of 'algorithmic transparency' and 'explainability' (XAI), as clinicians are more likely to trust and adopt tools that can provide a clear rationale for their output—for example, by highlighting specific regions of a medical image or data points that led to a diagnosis. Other systemic hurdles include the need to address data privacy concerns, the mitigation of algorithmic bias to ensure equitable patient care, and the management of AI integration into clinical workflows to prevent increasing clinician burnout. This reflects a broader tension between the efficiency gains provided by AI and the necessity of rigorous human oversight to maintain patient safety.

Simultaneously, the landscape of AI education and ethics in 2025 is marked by a tension between rapid adoption and persistent institutional gaps. According to 2025 reports from the AI Index, there is a significant disconnect between the desire for responsible AI and the actual implementation of ethics in practice. This disconnect is mirrored in academic focus; while general computer science (CS) remains a staple of technical education, there is a growing emphasis on AI-specific literacy and specialized degrees. However, the integration of AI into K-12 and higher education curricula varies wildly by region.

In the United States, while healthcare and finance sectors are leading the adoption of AI-driven workflows, regulatory hurdles remain. The global workforce is experiencing a 'skills gap,' where the demand for AI-competent professionals far outstrips the supply of graduates from traditional computer science programs. To bridge this gap, there has been an increase in short-term certifications and 'bootcamp' style learning, which exist alongside traditional academic degrees such as Bachelor's, Master's, and professional certifications. These shorter, specialized certification programs have become key for rapid skill acquisition in a market with rapidly growing demand.

Demographic disparities remain a central challenge in technical education. There is a significant disparity in gender representation across various technical fields and AI-related degrees. In the U.S., the state of K-12 computer science education shows mixed progress. While the percentage of schools offering computer science courses is growing, there is a notable disparity in the quality and availability of these courses across different demographics. Specifically, in the U20 population, there is a significant gap in computer science enrollment, with enrollment rates in some regions or demographics being significantly lower than others. While student interest in computer science remains high, the transition from introductory courses to advanced coursework is a critical bottleneck, often hindered by a lack of qualified teachers and systemic barriers.

At the higher education level, universities are adapting to the overall prevalence of generative AI. University policies are evolving from outright bans to guided integration, with an emphasis on the need for AI literacy among both students and faculty. This shift is focused on policy development, AI-assisted learning, and the challenge of maintaining academic integrity.

From a global perspective, there is a trend of 'AI Sovereignty,' where nations such as France, the UAE, and China are investing billions of dollars into domestic compute clusters and foundational models to reduce dependency on US-based providers like OpenAI, Google, and Meta. This geopolitical shift is driving a diversification of the hardware supply chain, which remains heavily reliant on NVIDIA GPUs.

Regarding the integration of AI into national curricula, some countries are more aggressive than the United States. China and several European nations have introduced AI modules at the primary and secondary education levels. In contrast, the U.S. faces a significant gap in AI education; while the government has emphasized AI literacy at the policy level, there is a lack of standardized AI curricula in schools, and implementation varies widely. 

Across all levels of education, a fundamental pedagogical challenge remains: the pedagogical framework for teaching AI—balancing theory, ethics, and practice—remains underdeveloped. Industry-led initiatives often fill the gap where public education falls short, but this frequently leads to an uneven distribution of AI skills across different socioeconomic groups.
block-L1-005.summary: In 2025, AI in healthcare is utilized for radiology (nodule detection and fracture identification in images up to 100,000 images), pathology, and cardiology, while the FDA's Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) streamline updates. Simultaneously, global AI education is marked by a 'skills gap' and 'AI Sovereignty' investments by France, the UAE, and China to reduce reliance on NVIDIA GPUs and US-based providers.

block-L1-006.context:
The current state of Artificial Intelligence in 2025 is defined by a complex interplay between technical development, economic investment, and operational stability. A primary tension exists between 'capabilities'—the model's utility and power—and 'safety'—the mitigation of risks associated with the model's output. While safety interventions are designed to prevent harm, they can inadvertently degrade a model's core reasoning capabilities or overall performance. To mitigate these risks, developers implement 'red teaming' and various guardrails to prevent the generation of harmful content. However, a known trade-off exists where over-tuning for safety can lead to 'refusal' behavior, where the model declines to answer even benign requests.

Technical safety and alignment are further complicated by the emergence of 'sycophancy' in Large Language Models (LLMs), defined as the tendency for models to mirror a user's views regardless of the actual accuracy of the information. This creates a significant challenge for the process of alignment, which aims to ensure that model outputs are aligned with human values and intentions.

From an economic perspective, the AI landscape in 2025 is marked by a high concentration of capital. Global investment is led by the United States, which dominates in both the scale and volume of funding. In comparisons of private investment, the U.S. significantly exceeded the totals of other leading countries. This dominance is further evidenced by the number of AI 'unicorns'—startups valued over $1 billion—where the U.S. maintains a dominant lead, acting as a proxy for the intensity of private capital flow. Growth in the sector is driven primarily by a small number of high-valuation firms, with a notable shift in investment trends moving from general-purpose AI research toward 'applied AI' and 'vertical AI'. Vertical AI refers to solutions tailored for specific industries such as healthcare, law, and finance, evidenced by increased funding for startups that integrate LLMs into specialized professional workflows. Despite this overall growth, investors are now demanding clearer paths to profitability and revenue generation, rather than funding based on technical novelty alone.

Public sector investment and funding patterns for AI between 2014 and 2024 in the United States reveal a detailed breakdown of spending instruments. Funding is categorized by grants, contracts, and loans, with grant funding historically being the primary mechanism for AI research. While contract funding for specific deliverables has grown, loans remain a less common instrument for AI-related initiatives. In contrast, Europe's AI funding is heavily influenced by the 'AI Act' and various Horizon Europe programs, emphasizing 'trustworthy AI' and public-interest applications. Globally, there is a trend toward increasing the scale of investments in AI infrastructure, specifically compute and data, and a shift toward public-private partnerships to accelerate deployment.

Public sentiment toward AI varies significantly by region and demographic. In the United States, there is a notable gap between the views of experts and the general public; while experts tend to be more optimistic about AI's capabilities, a significant portion of the general population expresses concern over job displacement and ethics. In the US market, a significant portion of the general population views AI as a risk to employment, whereas in other markets, the focus is more on the augmentation of human labor. Conversely, regions like Asia often show higher levels of optimism regarding AI's role in economic growth and productivity. While global awareness of AI is high, trust in AI systems remains low, particularly in developed economies where privacy and algorithmic bias are primary concerns.

In the realm of autonomous vehicles, the United States has experienced a mix of growth and challenges. While mileage for robotaxis has increased in cities like Phoenix and San Francisco, safety incidents have prompted some industry players to re-evaluate the timeline for 'driverless' or 'Level 4' autonomy. This reflects a broader tension between the rapid deployment of AI systems and the development of safety frameworks. There is a noted gap between deployment speed and the simultaneous development of corresponding safety benchmarks or oversight mechanisms, where many organizations are integrating AI but only a smaller fraction have established rigorous safety benchmarks.

AI governance is characterized by a global gap in enforcement. While several jurisdictions have begun introducing AI-specific legislation to mandate transparency and risk assessments, global governance approaches vary by jurisdiction. Some nations adopt a 'light-touch' approach to foster industry growth and innovation, while others move toward mandatory compliance and certification processes designed to ensure public safety and trust. This is most evident in the emergence of specific AI acts and guidelines, such as those in the European Union (EU), which aim to categorize AI risks and mandate audits for high-risk systems. Specifically, the EU AI Act represents a significant regulatory effort to categorize AI risks and mandate transparency, and the EU AI Office has been established to oversee compliance.

To address these challenges, the Responsible AI (RAI) framework has been developed, focusing on the monitoring and evaluation of AI systems through five established dimensions: (1) Data & Privacy, ensuring data quality, provenance, and user privacy protection; (2) Safety & Robustness, evaluating a model's resistance to adversarial attacks, stability, and avoidance of harmful content; (3) Fairness & Bias, testing for disparate impact and ensuring equitable performance across demographic groups; (4) Transparency & Explainability, which assesses the model's decision-making process; and (5) Human-AI Interaction, which evaluates the interface efficacy and safety. To operationalize these dimensions, the framework utilizes gold-standard benchmarks: 'AdvBench' and 'Do-Not-Answer' for safety and robustness (testing harmfulness and refusal behavior); 'Bbenchmark' and 'ToxiGen' for fairness (identifying social biases and toxicities); and 'TruthfulQA' for explainability (assessing factual accuracy and hallucinations).

Because LLMs are dynamic, the framework emphasizes the need for continuous red-teaming-based evaluation rather than relying solely on static tests. The current state of Responsible AI is further defined by the intersection of organizational implementation, academic research, and government governance. Organizational adoption of RAI frameworks is increasing, but maturity levels vary. According to survey data comparing 2024 and 2025, the average maturity score for RAI frameworks has risen from 2.5 to 2.8. While 62% of organizations have an established RAI framework (a slight increase from 59% the previous year), only 15% of organizations surveyed are categorized as 'high maturity' organizations, defined as those scoring 4 or higher.

In terms of implementation, the most common RAI activities are conducting impact assessments (54%) and the establishment of governance committees (48%). However, critical gaps in operationalization remain: only 28% of organizations report having a formal process for monitoring AI systems in production. There is a clear correlation between high-maturity organizations and the use of advanced technical techniques such as red-teaming and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Challenges hindering RAI implementation are primarily focused on talent and definition; 42% of organizations cited a lack of specialized talent as a primary challenge, and 38% cited the difficulty in defining clear, measurable metrics for 'fairness' and 'safety'.

Academic research has shifted toward frameworks that prioritize fairness, transparency, and safety, with an increasing focus on the societal impacts of AI, specifically algorithmic bias and the environmental cost associated with training large models.

Regarding the regulatory environment in the United States, 2025 survey data indicates a general consensus that current regulatory efforts are insufficient. Across various demographics, users are more likely to believe that the government is not doing enough to regulate AI than to believe it is over-regulating. This perceived insufficiency is observed across most measured groups, with lower percentages reporting belief in over-regulation. Specifically, among individuals with a college education, those with a higher education level, and older populations, there is a stronger tendency to view AI regulation as lagging. Political affiliation also plays a role, with both Democrats and Republicans showing a lean toward the need for more regulation, though the intensity of this feeling varies.

In the United States, the landscape of AI governance is characterized by a complex interplay between state-level and federal-level legislative activity. There is a persistent tension between these two tiers of governance; while some state-level laws focus on consumer protection and transparency, others pursue more comprehensive regulatory frameworks. For example, Utah passed legislation to regulate AI use in specific sectors, and California introduced and debated a landmark AI safety bill. The overarching challenge remains the inherent difficulty of regulating a rapidly evolving technology where traditional legislative cycles are often slower than the technical advancements they seek to govern. To mitigate this, there is a recognized need for inter-agency and inter-state cooperation to build a cohesive regulatory environment that balances the drive for innovation with essential safety and ethical considerations.

U.S. government policy has undergone a significant shift in strategic priorities between 2020 and 2025. The approach transitioned from an initial focus on safety and risk mitigation toward a more aggressive promotion of AI development. This pivot is marked by the implementation of a new policy framework specifically designed to accelerate AI innovation and maintain U.S. leadership in the face of global competition. The U.S. government has moved toward a 'pro-innovation' stance, shifting from a period of cautious regulatory oversight to a period focused on the active removal of barriers to development. This shift in priority is evident in the changing directives of federal agencies and the changing nature of the executive orders issued between 2020 and 2025, which have pivoted from managing AI risks to ensuring that the United States remains the primary global hub for AI research and deployment.

From a global perspective, the pursuit of national AI sovereignty is a strategic imperative. 'Sovereign AI' emphasizes that nations should develop, deploy, and run their own AI models using domestic data, computing resources, and a domestic workforce to fundamentally reduce dependency on foreign technology. To achieve this, governments are investing heavily in sovereign AI infrastructure, including the development of high-performance computing resources such as GPU clusters, and the creation of specialized datasets. A critical component of this sovereignty is the use of local-language datasets to ensure that AI models are culturally and linguistically aligned with the specific needs and values of the population they serve, avoiding the pitfalls of foreign-developed models that may not capture cultural nuances.

Global approach to AI sovereignty and regulation is defined by a balance between openness and other forms of protectionism. Some nations leverage open-source models to accelerate the pace of innovation, while other countries implement strict controls over data and model weights to protect national security and economic interests. This duality reflects the broader global competition for AI supremacy, where the integration of sovereign infrastructure, linguistic alignment, and a pro-innovation policy shift—as seen in the US—serves as a primary mechanism for ensuring national autonomy and economic stability in the AI era.

Regarding the workforce and skills, AI skill acquisition is being tracked via the prevalence of AI-related skills on LinkedIn profiles, showing a surge in demand. However, there is a noted 'compute divide,' where a few large companies control the vast majority of high-end GPUs, limiting the the ability of smaller entities to train frontier models.

Finally, there is a recurring technical failure in the system operational perspective regarding the interface between the user and the LLM, specifically in API or structured output systems. Users have reported a specific Python 'AttributeError' identified as ('NoneType' object has no attribute 'model_dump'). This error occurs when a function designed to return a Pydantic model or similar object returns `None` instead, and the subsequent call to `.model_dump()` (a Pydantic v2 method) is called on that `None` object. This indicates a technical failure in the backend processing of the response, which prevents the user from receiving the expected structured data in a valid JSON format matching a required schema, leading to requests for system-level error correction.

In terms of the economic output, while generative AI has boosted productivity in coding and writing, its impact on broader economic output is still being measured, with a notable gap between corporate optimism and actual implementation. This aligns with the investment shift toward 'vertical AI' for specialized professional workflows in healthcare, law, and finance, and the demand for clearer paths to profitability over technical novelty.
block-L1-006.summary: The 2025 AI landscape is marked by a tension between capabilities and safety, with the U.S. dominating in private investment and 'unicorns' while shifting toward a 'pro-innovation' policy from 2020-2025. Global efforts focus on 'Sovereign AI' and the Responsible AI (RAI) framework, which has seen average organizational maturity scores rise from 2.5 to 2.8.

   AI INDEX REPORT 2026
The AI Index is an independent initiative at the Stanford Institute for Human-
Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI).
The AI Index was conceived within the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial 
Intelligence (AI100).

Welcome to the ninth edition of the AI Index report. As AI continues to advance rapidly, the question 
becomes whether the systems built around it can keep up. Governance frameworks, evaluation methods, 
education systems, and the data infrastructure needed to track AI’s impact are struggling to match the pace 
of the technology itself. That gap—between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it—runs 
through every chapter of this year’s report. New in this edition, the report tracks how AI is being tested 
more ambitiously across reasoning, safety, and real-world task execution, and why those measurements are 
increasingly difficult to rely on. It also features new estimates of generative AI’s economic value alongside 
emerging evidence of its labor market effects, an analytical framework on AI sovereignty, and a science 
chapter developed in collaboration with Schmidt Sciences. For the first time, the report features standalone 
chapters on AI in science and AI in medicine, reflecting AI’s growing impact across these two domains.
For close to a decade, the AI Index has worked to bring reliable global data to a field that is evolving faster 
than most efforts to measure it. The report equips policymakers, researchers, executives, journalists, and the 
public with the necessary evidence to make informed decisions about AI. As the technology moves deeper 
into classrooms, clinics, and legislatures—and reshapes how people work, learn, and govern—the cost of 
incomplete data continues to rise.
In a field where much data is produced by organizations with a stake in the technology’s success, the demand 
for neutral and rigorous measurement continues to grow. The AI Index remains independent and focused on 
revealing the long-term patterns underneath the headlines. The report is relied on by governments, research 
institutions, and companies around the world, and referenced by media outlets and in academic papers.
The pages that follow offer the most comprehensive, independently sourced picture of AI’s trajectory that 
is available. They also make clear where that picture remains incomplete—because what we cannot yet 
measure matters just as much as what we can.

3
A year ago, this report documented AI’s arrival as a mainstream force. This year’s data shows what 
happens after arrival.
This is a technology that has reached mass adoption faster than the personal computer or the internet. 
Generative AI hit nearly 53% population-level adoption within three years. Leading AI companies are 
reaching meaningful revenue scale in a fraction of the time it took previous technology generations, 
and global corporate investment more than doubled in 2025. Organizational adoption rose to 88%, and 
early estimates suggest the consumer value of generative AI has grown substantially within a year.
The data does not point 
in a single direction. It 
reveals a field that is 
scaling faster than the 
systems around it 
can adapt.
“
Message from 
the Co-chairs
INTRODUCTION  |  AI INDEX REPORT 2026
At the technical frontier, leading models are now 
nearly indistinguishable from one another. 
Open-weight models are more competitive than 
ever. But as models converge, the tools used to 
evaluate them are struggling to stay relevant. 
Benchmarks are saturating, frontier labs are 
disclosing less, and independent testing does not 
always confirm what developers report.
The chapters that follow trace what this scale 
of activity and capability means in practice. In 
science, AI shifted from accelerating individual 
research steps to attempting full replacement 
of entire workflows. In medicine, clinical AI 
tools moved from pilot programs to broader 
deployment, with systems like ambient AI scribes 
scaling across health systems.
Governments around the world acted on AI in 2025, but not in the same direction. The EU AI Act’s first 
prohibitions took effect, while the United States shifted toward deregulation. Japan, South Korea, and 
Italy each passed national AI laws, and more than half of newly adopted national AI strategies came 
from developing countries entering the policy landscape for the first time. AI sovereignty emerged as a 
central organizing principle across all of these efforts. The public is also navigating competing signals. 
Global optimism about AI rose in 2025, but so did nervousness.
The data does not point in a single direction. It reveals a field that is scaling faster than the systems 
around it can adapt. We encourage you to explore and decide for yourself.
Yolanda Gil and Raymond Perrault 
Co-chairs, AI Index Report

AI INDEX REPORT 2026
1
AI capability is not plateauing. It is accelerating and reaching more people than 
ever. Industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models in 2025, and several of those models 
now meet or exceed human baselines on PhD-level science questions, multimodal reasoning, and 
competition mathematics. On a key coding benchmark—SWE-bench Verified—performance rose 
from 60% to near 100% of meeting the human baseline in a single year. Organizational adoption 
reached 88%, and 4 in 5 university students now use generative AI.
2
The U.S.-China AI model performance gap has effectively closed. U.S. and Chinese 
models have traded the lead multiple times since early 2025. In February 2025, DeepSeek-R1 
briefly matched the top U.S. model, and as of March 2026 Anthropic’s top model leads by just 
2.7%. The U.S. still produces more top-tier AI models and higher-impact patents, while China leads 
in publication volume, citations, patent output, and industrial robot installations. South Korea 
stands out for its innovation density, leading the world in AI patents per capita.
3
The United States hosts the most AI data centers, with the majority of their chips 
fabricated by one Taiwanese foundry. The United States hosts 5,427 data centers, more 
than 10 times any other country, and it consumes more energy than any other country. A single 
company, TSMC, fabricates almost every leading AI chip, making the global AI hardware supply 
chain dependent on one foundry in Taiwan—though a TSMC-U.S. expansion began operations in 
2025.
4
AI models can win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad 
but cannot reliably tell time—an example of what researchers call the jagged 
frontier of AI. Gemini Deep Think earned a gold medal at IMO, yet the top model reads analog 
clocks correctly just 50.1% of the time. AI agents made a leap from 12% to ~66% task success on 
OSWorld, which tests agents on real computer tasks across operating systems, though they still 
fail roughly 1 in 3 attempts on structured benchmarks.
5
Robots still fail at most household tasks, even as they excel in controlled 
environments. Robots succeed in only 12% of household tasks, highlighting how far AI is from 
mastering the physical world. On RLBench, robotic manipulation in software-based simulations 
has reached 89.4% success, but the gap between predictable lab settings and unpredictable 
household environments is wide.
6
Responsible AI is not keeping pace with AI capability, with safety benchmarks 
lagging and incidents rising sharply.  Almost all leading frontier AI model developers 
report results on capability benchmarks, but reporting on responsible AI benchmarks remains 
spotty. Documented AI incidents rose to 362, up from 233 in 2024. Adding to the challenge, recent 
research found that improving one responsible AI dimension, such as safety, can degrade another, 
such as accuracy.
Top Takeaways

10
TOP TAKEAWAYS  |  AI INDEX REPORT 2026
7
The United States leads in AI investment, but its ability to attract global talent 
is declining. U.S. private AI investment reached $285.9 billion in 2025, more than 23 times 
the $12.4 billion invested in China—though looking at just private investment figures likely 
understates China’s total AI spending, given its government guidance funds. The U.S. also led in 
entrepreneurial activity with 1,953 newly funded AI companies in 2025, more than 10 times the 
next closest country. However, the number of AI researchers and developers moving to the U.S. 
has dropped 89% since 2017, with an 80% decline in the last year alone.
8
AI adoption is spreading at historic speed, and consumers are deriving 
substantial value from tools they often access for free. Generative AI reached 53% 
population adoption within three years, faster than the PC or the internet, though the pace 
varies by country and correlates strongly with GDP per capita. Some show higher-than-expected 
adoption, such as Singapore (61%) and the United Arab Emirates (54%), while the U.S. ranks 24th at 
28.3%. The estimated value of generative AI tools to U.S. consumers reached $172 billion annually 
by early 2026, with the median value per user tripling between 2025 and 2026.
9
Productivity gains from AI are appearing in many of the same fields where entry-
level employment is starting to decline. Studies show productivity gains of 14% to 26% in 
customer support and software development, with weaker or negative effects in tasks requiring 
more judgment. AI agent deployment remains in single digits across nearly all business functions. 
In software development, where AI’s measured productivity gains are clearest, U.S. developers 
ages 22 to 25 saw employment fall nearly 20% from 2024, even as the headcount for older 
developers continues to grow.
10
AI’s environmental footprint is expanding alongside its capabilities. Grok 4’s 
estimated training emissions reached 72,816 tons of CO2 equivalent. AI data center power 
capacity rose to 29.6 GW, comparable to New York state at peak demand, and annual GPT-4o 
inference water use alone may exceed the drinking water needs of 1.2 million people.
11
AI models for science can outperform human scientists, though bigger models 
do not always perform better. Frontier models outperform human chemists on average 
on ChemBench, yet they score below 20% on replication in astrophysics and 33% on Earth 
observation questions. A 111-million-parameter protein language model, MSAPairformer, beat 
previous leading methods on ProteinGym, and a 200-million-parameter genomics model, GPN-
Star, outperformed a model nearly 200 times larger. Most AI foundation models for science come 
from cross-sector collaborations, in contrast with the industry-dominated landscape of general-
purpose AI.
12
AI is transforming clinical care, but rigorous evidence remains limited. AI tools 
that automatically generate clinical notes from patient visits saw substantial adoption in 2025. 
Across multiple hospital systems, physicians reported up to 83% less time spent writing notes and 
significant reductions in burnout. Beyond certain tools, however, the evidence base for clinical AI 
remains thin. A review of more than 500 clinical AI studies found that nearly half relied on exam-
style questions rather than real patient data, with only 5% using real clinical data.

15
Formal education is lagging behind AI, but people are learning AI skills at every 
stage of life. Over 80% of U.S. high school and college students now use AI for school-related 
tasks, but only half of middle and high schools have AI policies in place, and just 6% of teachers 
say those policies are clear. Outside the classroom, AI engineering skills are accelerating fastest 
in the United Arab Emirates, Chile, and South Africa. The number of new AI PhDs in the U.S. 
and Canada increased 22% from 2022 to 2024, the PhDs that make up that increase took jobs in 
academia, not in industry.
AI sovereignty is becoming a defining feature of national policy, but capabilities 
remain uneven, even as open-source development helps to redistribute who 
participates. National AI strategies are expanding, particularly among developing economies, 
and state-backed investments in AI supercomputing are rising in parallel—a sign of growing 
ambitions for domestic control over AI ecosystems. Yet model production remains concentrated 
in the U.S. and China. Open-source development is starting to redistribute participation, with 
contributions from the rest of the world now outpacing Europe and approaching the United States 
on GitHub, fueling more linguistically diverse models and benchmarks.
AI experts and the public have very different perspectives on the technology’s 
future, and global trust in institutions to manage AI is fragmented. When it comes 
to how people do their jobs, 73% of experts expect a positive impact, compared with just 23% 
of the public, a 50-point gap. Similar divides appear for AI’s impact on the economy and medical 
care. Globally, trust in governments to regulate AI varies. Among surveyed countries, the United 
States reported the lowest level of trust in its own government to regulate AI, at 31%. Globally, the 
EU is trusted more than the United States or China to regulate AI effectively.

Overview
The resources powering AI development continued to grow 
in 2025, but fewer notable models were released than the 
year before, and the systems at the frontier are increasingly 
concentrated among a small number of organizations. 
Industry now accounts for over 90% of notable AI models, 
and the most capable systems are also the least transparent, 
with training code, dataset sizes, and parameter counts 
increasingly withheld. The computing power behind these 
models has grown roughly 3.3 times per year since 2022, yet 
almost all of it flows through a single chip foundry in Taiwan, 
making the global hardware supply chain fragile. Open-
source development and AI publications continued to grow, 
and the research landscape is becoming more geographically 
distributed. China now leads in publication volume, citation 
share, and patent grants, while smaller countries like 
Switzerland and Singapore lead in AI researchers per capita. 
Yet some dimensions of the field have not changed at all. 
Gender gaps in AI talent remain deeply entrenched, with no 
meaningful progress in any country since 2010. This chapter 
covers the research and development pipeline, from the 
landscape of AI models through the compute, data centers, 
energy, and open-source software that support them, to the 
broader research ecosystem of publications, patents, and talent.
